questions.fig: Photo of a spherical storage tank; in (c) a tank made of a cylinder of length $h$ m with a hemisphere at each end.

parts.q: A company has a spherical storage tank. The diameter of the tank is 12 m. Write down the radius of the tank.

idea.title: Radius and diameter
idea.text: The diameter goes all the way across a circle or sphere, through the centre. The radius only goes from the centre to the edge, so it is half the diameter.

steps.say: The radius is half of the diameter, so divide 12 by 2.
So the radius of the tank is 6 m.

parts.tip: Almost every sphere, cylinder and cone formula uses the radius. If you are given the diameter, halve it first.

parts.q: Find the volume of the tank, correct to the nearest $\text{m}^3$.
parts.scheme: $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi(6)^3 = 904.779 \approx 905$ m³. Answer in terms of $\pi$ ($288\pi$) gets partial credit only. Using $\frac{22}{7}$ (905.14) or 3.14 (904.32) accepted.

idea.title: Volume of a sphere
idea.text: Volume is how much space a solid takes up, measured in cubic units (m³). For a sphere the formula is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$. It is in the Formulae and Tables booklet, so you only need to put the radius in.

steps.say: Write down the formula for the volume of a sphere from the tables booklet.
Put in the radius, r = 6. Cube it first: 6 × 6 × 6 = 216.
Now multiply it out on the calculator: 4 ÷ 3 × π × 216.
Round to the nearest whole number. So the volume is 905 m³.

parts.tip: Volume units are always cubed: m³. Type the whole calculation into the calculator in one go so you don't round too early.

parts.q: The company paints the outside curved surface of the spherical tank. Find the curved surface area of the tank, correct to one decimal place.
parts.scheme: $4\pi r^2 = 4\pi(6)^2 = 452.389 \approx 452.4$ m². ($144\pi$ only gets high partial credit.)

idea.title: Surface area of a sphere
idea.text: Surface area is the amount of skin on the outside of a solid, measured in square units (m²). For a sphere it is $4\pi r^2$, which is also in the tables booklet.

steps.say: Write the formula for the curved surface area of a sphere.
Put in r = 6 and square it: 6 × 6 = 36.
Work it out and round to one decimal place. So the curved surface area is 452.4 m².

parts.tip: Area is squared (m²), volume is cubed (m³). Check you used the right power of r.

parts.q: The curved surface is painted with a special paint. One litre of paint will cover $3{\cdot}5\ \text{m}^2$. Find how many litres of paint are used, correct to the nearest litre.
parts.scheme: $\frac{452.4}{3.5} = 129.2 \approx 129$ or 130 litres. Accept a consistent answer from (b)(i).

steps.say: Each litre covers 3.5 m². To find how many litres cover the whole 452.4 m², divide the area by 3.5.
Work it out and round to the nearest litre. So about 129 litres of paint are used.

parts.tip: "How many fit into" means divide.

parts.q: The paint is sold in 25 litre tins. Each tin costs €180. Find the total cost of the paint.
parts.scheme: $\frac{129}{25} = 5.17$, so 6 tins; $6 \times \text{€}180 = \text{€}1080$. Accept a consistent answer from (b)(ii).

steps.say: Find how many 25-litre tins are needed: divide the litres by 25.
5 tins is not quite enough paint, and you can't buy part of a tin, so round UP to 6 tins.
Multiply by the price of one tin. So the paint costs €1080.

parts.tip: When you buy tins, boxes or buses, always round UP — 5.16 tins means you need 6.

parts.q: At another site the company has a differently-shaped tank with the same volume. This tank has hemispherical ends and a cylindrical mid-section of length $h$ m, as shown. The radius of each hemispherical end is $4{\cdot}5$ m. Find the volume of one hemispherical end, correct to the nearest $\text{m}^3$.

idea.title: A hemisphere is half a sphere
idea.text: "Hemi" means half. So a hemisphere's volume is half of $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, which is $\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$.

steps.say: A hemisphere is half a sphere, so take half of the sphere formula.
Put in r = 4.5.
Work it out and round to the nearest whole number. So one hemispherical end holds 191 m³.

parts.q: Find the length, $h$, of the cylindrical section, correct to one decimal place.

idea.title: Finding a missing length from a volume
idea.text: If you know the total volume, write "the parts add up to the total" as an equation. The unknown length is the only letter left, so you solve for it like any equation.

steps.say: This tank has the same volume as the sphere, 905 m³. It is made of two hemispheres plus a cylinder, so those add up to 905.
The cylinder has the same radius, 4.5 m. Put that in, and work out the two hemispheres: 2 × 191 = 382.
Take 382 from both sides, so only the cylinder is left on the left.
π × 4.5² is just a number (about 63.62). Divide both sides by it to get h on its own.
Round to one decimal place. So the cylindrical section is 8.2 m long.

parts.tip: Write the equation "parts = total" first — the examiner gives marks for setting it up even if the arithmetic slips.

questions.stem: The Atomium in Brussels is one of Belgium's most famous landmarks. It consists of 9 identical spheres joined by two types of cylindrical pipes.
questions.fig: Photo of the Atomium: 9 metal spheres joined by cylindrical pipes.

parts.q: The Atomium is modelled on an iron atom that has been magnified 165 billion times. Given that a billion is a thousand million, write 165 billion in the form $a \times 10^n$, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, and $1 \le a < 10$.

idea.title: Scientific notation
idea.text: $a \times 10^n$ means: a number between 1 and 10, times a power of 10. The power tells you how many places the decimal point moves.

steps.say: A thousand is 10³ and a million is 10⁶, so a billion (a thousand million) is 10³ × 10⁶ = 10⁹. Add the powers when you multiply.
So 165 billion is 165 × 10⁹.
165 is not between 1 and 10. Write 165 as 1.65 × 10², then add the powers again.
So 165 billion = 1.65 × 10¹¹.

parts.tip: Check: 'a' must be at least 1 and less than 10. 16.5 × 10¹⁰ is the right size but loses marks.

parts.q: The diameter of each sphere in the Atomium is 18 metres. Find the radius of each sphere.

idea.title: Radius and diameter
idea.text: The diameter goes all the way across through the centre; the radius goes from the centre to the edge. Radius = diameter ÷ 2.

steps.say: Halve the diameter to get the radius.
So each sphere has a radius of 9 m.

parts.q: Find the volume of each sphere, correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: Volume of a sphere
idea.text: The tables booklet gives $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$. You only need the radius.

steps.say: Write the formula and put in r = 9.
9³ = 9 × 9 × 9 = 729, and four-thirds of 729 is 972.
Work it out and round to 2 decimal places. So each sphere has a volume of 3053.63 m³.

parts.tip: Use the π button, not 3.14, unless the question tells you to.

parts.q: Find the combined surface area of all 9 spheres in the Atomium, correct to the nearest $\text{m}^2$.

idea.title: Surface area of a sphere
idea.text: The skin of a sphere has area $4\pi r^2$ (in the tables booklet). For several identical spheres, find one and multiply.

steps.say: Find the surface area of one sphere first, with r = 9.
There are 9 identical spheres, so multiply by 9.
Work it out and round to the nearest whole number. So the 9 spheres have a surface area of 9161 m².

parts.tip: Keep π in until the very end, then round once.

parts.q: Each of the 8 cylindrical pipes extending from the centre sphere has a radius of $1{\cdot}65$ m and a length of 23 m. Find the sum of the curved surface areas of all 8 pipes, correct to the nearest $\text{m}^2$.

idea.title: Curved surface area of a cylinder
idea.text: If you unroll the curved side of a cylinder you get a rectangle. One side is the height $h$, the other is the distance around the circle, $2\pi r$. So the curved area is $2\pi r h$.

steps.say: A pipe is a cylinder. Its length is the height h = 23 and its radius is r = 1.65. Use the curved surface area formula.
Put in the numbers for one pipe.
There are 8 pipes, so multiply by 8.
Work it out and round. So the 8 pipes have a curved surface area of 1908 m².

parts.tip: A pipe's 'length' is the cylinder's height h.

parts.q: The other 12 cylindrical pipes connect the outer spheres to each other. Each pipe has a radius of $1{\cdot}45$ m. All 12 pipes are equal in length. The sum of the curved surface areas of the 12 pipes is $3170\ \text{m}^2$. Find the length of one pipe. Give your answer correct to the nearest metre.

idea.title: Working backwards to a missing length
idea.text: When the area is given and a length is missing, write the formula = the area you know, then solve for the missing letter.

steps.say: The 12 pipes are identical, so one pipe has a twelfth of the area.
Set the curved area of one pipe, 2πrh, equal to that, with r = 1.45.
2π × 1.45 is just a number (about 9.11). Divide both sides by it to get h alone.
Round to the nearest metre. So each pipe is 29 m long.

parts.tip: Write the equation with the formula on one side and the given area on the other — that alone gets you partial credit.

parts.q: The curved surfaces of the 20 pipes and 9 spheres are covered in stainless steel. Stainless steel costs €70 per square metre. Use the areas you have calculated or have been given above to find the approximate cost of the stainless steel required to resurface the Atomium.

steps.say: Add up all the curved areas: the 8 pipes from (d)(i), the 12 pipes (given), and the 9 spheres from (c).
Each square metre costs €70, so multiply by 70. So the steel costs about €996 730.

questions.topic: The trapezoidal rule (area of a field)
questions.fig: (a) A field with a curved edge cut into 8 strips of width 3 m; heights 4, 5·8, 7, 6·5, 6, 4·8, 6, 6·5, 8. (b) The same field cut into 6 strips of width 4 m; heights 4, 6·4, 6·9, 6, x, 6·2, 8.

parts.q: A field is divided into eight sections as shown below. The width of each section is 3 metres. The height, in metres, of each section is given in the diagram. Use the Trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of the field.

idea.title: The trapezoidal rule
idea.text: Cut the shape into strips of equal width $h$. Each strip is nearly a trapezium, so add up their areas. The tables booklet gives the shortcut: Area $\approx \frac{h}{2}[\text{first} + \text{last} + 2(\text{all the others})]$.

steps.say: Write the trapezoidal rule. h is the width of each strip, and the y's are the heights, read from left to right.
Here h = 3. The first height is 4 and the last is 8. Every height in between goes inside the bracket that gets doubled.
Add up the middle heights: they come to 42.6. Doubled, that is 85.2.
Finish: 1.5 × 97.2. So the area of the field is about 145.8 m².

parts.tip: Count the heights: 8 sections means 9 heights. Only the first and last are NOT doubled.

parts.q: The area of the same field was re-estimated by applying the Trapezoidal rule again. This time, a different section width (4 m) and a different set of section heights were used, as shown below. The area was found to be $145{\cdot}6\ \text{m}^2$. Use this information to find the value of the height marked $x$ on the diagram.

idea.title: Using the rule backwards
idea.text: If the area is given and one height is missing, fill in the rule as usual with $x$ for the missing height, set it equal to the area, and solve the equation.

steps.say: Fill in the rule with h = 4: first height 4, last height 8, and the middle heights (including x) doubled. Set it equal to the area, 145.6.
Tidy up: 4 ÷ 2 = 2, 4 + 8 = 12, and the known middle heights add to 25.5.
Multiply out the brackets, inside first.
Take 126 from both sides, then divide by 4.
So the missing height x is 4.9 m.

parts.tip: Getting the formula fully filled in with x earns most of the marks — then it is just solving an equation.

questions.topic: Construction; area of a square with a triangle removed
questions.fig: (b) A square of side $2k$ cm. In (b)(ii) a right-angled isosceles triangle with two sides of 20 cm and hypotenuse $2k$ cm is cut from the bottom-left corner of the square; the rest is shaded.

parts.q: Construct the triangle $ABC$, where $|AB| = 8$ cm, $|AC| = 5$ cm, and $|BC| = 7$ cm.

answer.show: Draw [AB] = 8 cm; arc of radius 5 cm from A and arc of radius 7 cm from B; they cross at C. Join and label A, B, C.

parts.scheme: Correct construction (tolerance ±0.25 cm) with sides or vertices labelled. Arcs must be shown; a rough pilot diagram alone gets low partial credit.

idea.title: Constructing a triangle from three sides
idea.text: A compass draws every point that is a fixed distance from its point. So an arc of radius 5 from A holds every point 5 cm from A. Where two arcs cross is the one point at the right distance from both.

steps.say: Draw a rough sketch first and label it, so you know which side is which.
Use your ruler to draw the base [AB] exactly 8 cm long. Label A and B.
Open the compass to 5 cm. Put the point on A and draw an arc above the line.
Open the compass to 7 cm. Put the point on B and draw an arc that crosses the first one. The crossing point is C.
Join A to C and B to C, and label C. Leave the arcs showing — the examiner needs to see them.

parts.tip: Never rub out your construction arcs.

parts.q: The diagram shows a square of side length $2k$ cm. Write down, in terms of $k$, an expression for the area of the square.
parts.scheme: Area $= (2k)^2 = 4k^2$ cm². Correct answer without work gets full credit.

idea.title: Area of a square
idea.text: Area of a square = side × side. That works with letters too: just multiply the numbers and the letters separately.

steps.say: Area of a square is side × side, and each side is 2k.
Multiply the numbers (2 × 2 = 4) and the letters (k × k = k²). So the area is 4k² cm².

parts.tip: (2k)² is 4k², not 2k² — the 2 gets squared too.

parts.q: An isosceles triangle with side lengths of 20 cm and hypotenuse of length $2k$ cm is removed from the square, as shown. Find the value of $k$ (correct to 2 decimal places) and the area of the remaining (shaded) section.

idea.title: Pythagoras finds a missing side
idea.text: In a right-angled triangle, (hypotenuse)² = (one side)² + (other side)². The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.

steps.say: The triangle has a right angle in the corner of the square, with two sides of 20 and hypotenuse 2k. Use Pythagoras.
Work out each side: (2k)² = 4k², and 400 + 400 = 800.
Divide by 4, then take the square root.
Now the area. The square's area is 4k² from part (i), and k² = 200, so it is 4 × 200 = 800 cm².
The triangle's area is half × base × height, with base and height both 20.
The shaded part is what is left: square minus triangle. So k = 14.14 and the shaded area is 600 cm².

parts.tip: Use k² = 200 for the square's area instead of the rounded 14.14 — you get the exact 600.

questions.topic: Cones: slant height, curved surface area and the net
questions.stem: Cones is a sculpture in the National Gallery of Australia. It consists of 14 identical steel cones arranged into pairs which are joined together as shown.
questions.fig: Photo of the sculpture (pairs of shiny steel cones joined at their points). In (c) the net of one cone: a sector of radius 5·03 m, arc length $p$ m and angle $\theta$ at the centre.

parts.q: The height of each cone is equal to the diameter of its base. If the radius of the base is $2{\cdot}25$ m, write the height of a cone.
parts.scheme: $h = 2 \times 2.25 = 4.5$ m. Correct answer without work gets full credit.

idea.title: The parts of a cone
idea.text: A cone has three lengths: the radius $r$ of its circular base, the vertical height $h$ from the base up to the tip, and the slant height $l$ along the sloping side. $h$, $r$ and $l$ make a right-angled triangle.

steps.say: The height equals the diameter, and the diameter is twice the radius.
So the height of each cone is 4.5 m.

parts.q: Show that, correct to 2 decimal places, the slant height, $l$, of a cone is $5{\cdot}03$ m.

idea.title: Slant height by Pythagoras
idea.text: Slice a cone down the middle: the height, the radius and the slant height form a right-angled triangle, with the slant height as the longest side. So $l^2 = h^2 + r^2$.

steps.say: Use Pythagoras on the triangle inside the cone: slant height² = height² + radius².
Put in h = 4.5 and r = 2.25.
Take the square root and round to 2 decimal places. That shows the slant height is 5.03 m.

parts.tip: In a 'show that' question, write every line of working and finish on the number they gave you.

parts.q: In order to maintain the steel's reflective shine, the surface is polished regularly. Find the curved surface area of the entire sculpture (14 cones). Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.scheme: CSA $= 14 \times \pi r l = 14 \times \pi(2.25)(5.03) = 497.77$ m². (One cone: 35.55 m².)

idea.title: Curved surface area of a cone
idea.text: The sloping skin of a cone has area $\pi r l$, where $l$ is the slant height (not the vertical height). It is in the tables booklet.

steps.say: The curved surface of one cone is πrl. Use the slant height l = 5.03, not the height.
That is 35.55… m² for one cone. There are 14 cones, so multiply by 14.
Round to 2 decimal places. So the whole sculpture has a curved surface area of 497.77 m².

parts.tip: Cone area uses l (slant); cone volume uses h (height). Don't mix them up.

parts.q: One litre of polish will cover $12{\cdot}25\ \text{m}^2$. Find how many litres are needed to polish the entire sculpture. Give your answer correct to the nearest litre.

steps.say: Each litre covers 12.25 m², so divide the total area by 12.25.
Round to the nearest litre. So 41 litres are needed.

parts.q: A container of polish contains 5 litres and costs $\text{A\textdollar}110$. Find the number of containers of polish that must be purchased in order to polish the entire sculpture and hence find the cost of the polish in euro ($\text{A\textdollar}1 = \text{€}0{\cdot}68$). Give your answer correct to the nearest euro.

steps.say: Each container holds 5 litres. Divide 41 by 5.
8 containers is not enough, so you must buy 9.
Find the cost in Australian dollars, then change to euro: each Australian dollar is worth €0.68, so multiply by 0.68.
Round to the nearest euro. So you buy 9 containers, costing €673.

parts.tip: Containers: round UP. Money: round as asked.

parts.q: The diagram (not to scale) shows the net of the outer surface of one of the cones of the sculpture. It is a sector of a circle of radius length $5{\cdot}03$ m with arc length $p$ m and angle $\theta$ at the centre, as shown below. Find $p$, the length of the arc of the sector. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.scheme: $p = 2\pi r = 2\pi(2.25) = 14.14$ m (the arc wraps around the base of the cone).

idea.title: The net of a cone
idea.text: Unroll the side of a cone and you get a sector of a circle. Its radius is the cone's slant height, and its curved edge (the arc) wraps exactly around the base circle. So the arc length = the base's circumference, $2\pi r$.

steps.say: When the sector is rolled up into the cone, the arc p goes once round the base circle. So p is the circumference of the base, with r = 2.25.
Work it out and round to 2 decimal places. So the arc is 14.14 m long.

parts.tip: Use the base radius 2.25 here, not 5.03 — the arc matches the BASE of the cone.

parts.q: Find $\theta$, the angle at the centre of the sector. Show all your working out. Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

idea.title: Arc length of a sector
idea.text: A sector with angle $\theta$ is the fraction $\frac{\theta}{360}$ of a full circle. So its arc is that fraction of the full circumference: arc $= \frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$.

steps.say: The sector has radius 5.03. Its arc is the fraction θ/360 of the full circle's circumference, and we know the arc is 14.14.
The full circumference 2π(5.03) is about 31.60. Multiply both sides by 360 and divide by 31.60.
Round to the nearest degree. So the angle at the centre is 161°.

parts.tip: Sector questions: arc = (θ/360) × 2πr and area = (θ/360) × πr². Learn both.

questions.topic: Area of a square inside a square; circumference of wheels
questions.fig: (a) Square ABCD of side 7 cm with a tilted square PQRS whose corners touch its sides; $|AQ| = 5$ cm along the bottom. (b) Two touching circles (wheels): $u$ of radius 4 cm and $v$ of radius 6 cm.

parts.q: The square $ABCD$ has sides of length 7 cm. The vertices of the square $PQRS$ lie on the perimeter of $ABCD$, as shown in the diagram, with $|AQ| = 5$ cm. Find the area of the square $PQRS$.
parts.scheme: Area $ABCD - 4(\text{area of } AQP) = 7 \times 7 - 4[\frac{1}{2}(5)(2)] = 49 - 20 = 29$ cm². Or: $|PQ|^2 = 5^2 + 2^2 = 29$, so area $= (\sqrt{29})^2 = 29$ cm².

idea.title: Area by subtraction
idea.text: When a shape is awkward, find the area of a simple shape around it and take away the pieces that are not part of it.

steps.say: The big square is 7 by 7, so its area is 49 cm².
Q splits the bottom side into 5 and 7 − 5 = 2. The tilted square cuts off 4 identical right-angled triangles in the corners, so each has sides 5 and 2. That means |AP| = |QB| = 2.
Each corner triangle has area half × base × height.
Take the 4 triangles away from the big square. So the area of PQRS is 29 cm².

parts.tip: Check with Pythagoras: |PQ|² = 5² + 2² = 29, and the area of a square is side², so 29 again.

parts.q: The circles $u$ and $v$ represent two wheels that are free to rotate about their centres, as shown. The radius of $u$ is 4 cm and the radius of $v$ is 6 cm. Find the length of the circumference of each circle. Give your answers in cm in terms of $\pi$.

idea.title: Circumference
idea.text: The circumference is the distance once around a circle: $2\pi r$. 'In terms of $\pi$' means leave the $\pi$ as a letter — don't turn it into a decimal.

steps.say: Circumference = 2πr. For u, r = 4.
For v, r = 6.
So u has circumference 8π cm and v has circumference 12π cm.

parts.tip: 'In terms of π' — write 8π, not 25.13.

parts.q: The wheels $u$ and $v$ are in non-slip contact and therefore the rotation of one causes the other to rotate. Find the number of complete rotations wheel $u$ makes if wheel $v$ completes 100 rotations.

idea.title: Wheels that touch
idea.text: If two wheels touch without slipping, their rims move the same distance. Each full turn moves a rim one circumference.

steps.say: In 100 turns, the rim of v moves 100 circumferences.
The rim of u moves the same distance. Each turn of u covers 8π, so divide.
So wheel u makes 150 complete rotations.

parts.tip: The π cancels — that's why they asked for answers in terms of π.

questions.topic: Volume of a gold sphere; margin of error and hypothesis test

parts.q: Find the volume of a solid sphere of radius $0{\cdot}3$ cm. Give your answer in $\text{cm}^3$, correct to 3 decimal places.
parts.scheme: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi(0.3)^3 = 0.113097 = 0.113$ cm³. (0.113097 without rounding loses 1 mark.)

idea.title: Volume of a sphere
idea.text: A sphere's volume is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ (in the tables booklet). Cube the radius, then multiply by $\frac{4}{3}$ and $\pi$.

steps.say: Write the sphere formula and put in r = 0.3.
0.3³ = 0.3 × 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.027. Then multiply by 4/3 and π.
Round to 3 decimal places. So the volume is 0.113 cm³.

parts.tip: Always round to what they ask: 3 decimal places here.

parts.q: The sphere is made of pure gold. Each $\text{cm}^3$ of pure gold weighs $19{\cdot}3$ grams. Find the number of grams of pure gold in the sphere. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

steps.say: Every 1 cm³ weighs 19.3 g, so multiply the volume by 19.3.
Round to 2 decimal places. So the sphere holds 2.18 g of gold.

parts.q: It is known that there are approximately $6{\cdot}02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms in 197 grams of pure gold. Find the number of atoms of pure gold in the sphere. Give your answer in the form $a \times 10^n$, where $1 \le a < 10$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and where $a$ is correct to 2 significant figures.
parts.scheme: 1 g contains $\frac{6.02 \times 10^{23}}{197}$ atoms, so 2.18 g contains $\frac{6.02 \times 10^{23}}{197} \times 2.18 = 6.7 \times 10^{21}$ atoms.

idea.title: Unitary method
idea.text: Find how much ONE unit gives, then multiply by how many units you have.

steps.say: Find the number of atoms in 1 gram: divide by 197.
The sphere is 2.18 g, so multiply by 2.18.
Round a to 2 significant figures. So there are about 6.7 × 10²¹ atoms.

parts.tip: Use the calculator's ×10ˣ button for 10²³ so the powers come out right.

parts.q: A survey was carried out on behalf of a television station to investigate the popularity of a certain show. A random sample of 1560 television viewers was surveyed. Find the margin of error of the survey. Give your answer as a percentage, correct to 1 decimal place.

idea.title: Margin of error
idea.text: A survey of $n$ people is only an estimate. At Ordinary Level the margin of error is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$: the bigger the sample, the smaller the error.

steps.say: Use the margin of error formula with n = 1560.
Change it to a percentage (× 100) and round to 1 decimal place. So the margin of error is 2.5%.

parts.q: In the survey, 546 of the 1560 viewers surveyed said that they liked the show. Use your answer to part b(i) above to create a 95% confidence interval for the percentage of viewers who liked the show.

idea.title: Confidence interval
idea.text: Take the sample percentage and go the margin of error below and above it. The true percentage is very likely (95%) in that range.

steps.say: Find the sample proportion: 546 out of 1560.
Go 2.5% either side of 35%.
So the 95% confidence interval is from 32.5% to 37.5%.

parts.q: An executive for the television station had claimed that 40% of viewers liked the show. Use your answer to part b(ii) above to conduct a hypothesis test, at the 5% level of significance, to test the executive's claim. State your null hypothesis, your alternative hypothesis and give your conclusion in the context of the question.

options: Reject the null hypothesis: the claim that 40% like the show is rejected
Do not reject the null hypothesis: the 40% claim stands

parts.scheme: $H_0: p = 40\%$; $H_1: p \ne 40\%$. $40\% \notin [32.5\%, 37.5\%]$, so reject $H_0$: the percentage of viewers who like the show is not 40% (reject the executive's claim).

idea.title: Hypothesis test with a confidence interval
idea.text: The null hypothesis $H_0$ is the claim being tested. If the claimed value is inside the confidence interval, keep it; if it is outside, reject it.

steps.say: Write the null hypothesis (the claim) and the alternative (the claim is wrong).
Check if 40% is inside the interval from (b)(ii). It is not: 40 is bigger than 37.5.
So reject the null hypothesis: the evidence says the percentage of viewers who like the show is not 40%, so the executive's claim is rejected.

parts.tip: Always finish with a sentence about the actual question (the show and the executive's claim), not just 'reject H₀'.

questions.topic: The trapezoidal rule from a scale diagram; changing units of speed
questions.stem: Harry draws a scale diagram of the portion of his garden that is covered in lawn. His diagram is shown below. Each box on the grid is 1 cm $\times$ $0{\cdot}5$ cm. Each cm on Harry's diagram represents 3 m. In order to estimate the area of the lawn Harry divides the diagram into eight sections.
questions.fig: A lawn-shaped curve on a grid (boxes 1 cm wide, 0·5 cm tall), cut by 7 vertical lines 1 cm apart into 8 sections; the ends are 0 at the left and right points.

parts.q: Use the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of the lawn using the scale: 1 cm = 3 m.

idea.title: The trapezoidal rule
idea.text: Cut the area into strips of equal width $h$ and measure the height at each cut. Area $\approx \frac{h}{2}[\text{first} + \text{last} + 2(\text{all the others})]$ — it is in the tables booklet.

steps.say: Change the diagram into real metres first. Each strip is 1 cm wide on the diagram, which is 3 m in real life. So h = 3.
Now measure each vertical line. A box is 0.5 cm tall, so 2 boxes = 1 cm = 3 m. The first line is 10 boxes = 5 cm = 15 m. Do the same for the others: 15, 18, 15, 12, 15, 18, 15 m. The two ends are 0.
Put them into the trapezoidal rule. First and last are both 0; all the rest are doubled.
The middle heights add to 108. Doubled, that is 216.
So the area of the lawn is about 324 m².

parts.tip: Convert every length to metres BEFORE using the rule; then the area comes out in m².

parts.q: Nuala can walk at a speed of $1{\cdot}6$ metres per second. Write this speed in kilometres per hour.

idea.title: Changing units of speed
idea.text: Change one unit at a time. Metres per second → metres per hour (× 3600, the seconds in an hour) → km per hour (÷ 1000, the metres in a km).

steps.say: In one second she walks 1.6 m. In one hour (60 × 60 = 3600 seconds) she walks 3600 times as far.
There are 1000 m in a km, so divide by 1000. So her speed is 5.76 km/h.

parts.tip: Sense check: walking speed of about 5 or 6 km/h is right.

questions.topic: Area and perimeter of a crescent; filling a cone
questions.fig: (a) A shaded crescent: a disc of radius 2·5 cm removed from a disc of radius 3 cm, touching on one side. (b) An upside-down cone, radius 7 cm, height 12 cm, being filled from a pipe.

parts.q: The crescent, shown in the shaded part of the diagram, was created by removing a disc of radius $2{\cdot}5$ cm from a disc of radius 3 cm. Find the area and the perimeter of the crescent. Give each answer correct to two decimal places.
parts.scheme: Area $= \pi(3)^2 - \pi(2.5)^2 = 9\pi - 6.25\pi = 8.64$ cm². Perimeter $= 2\pi(3) + 2\pi(2.5) = 6\pi + 5\pi = 34.56$ cm. (Answers in terms of $\pi$ get high partial credit.)

idea.title: Area vs perimeter of a cut-out shape
idea.text: Area is the space inside, so the cut-out disc is TAKEN AWAY. Perimeter is the length of the edge you would trace with a finger: that is the outside circle AND the inside circle, so both circumferences are ADDED.

steps.say: Area of a disc is πr². Find the big disc (r = 3) and the small disc (r = 2.5).
The crescent is what is left when the small disc is removed, so subtract.
For the perimeter, trace round the crescent: you go along the outer circle and back along the inner circle. Circumference is 2πr for each.
Both edges are part of the outline, so add them. So the area is 8.64 cm² and the perimeter is 34.56 cm.

parts.tip: Area: subtract the hole. Perimeter: add the hole's edge.

parts.q: An empty inverted cone of vertical height 12 cm and radius 7 cm is filled with water from a pipe. The water flows from the pipe at a steady rate of $0{\cdot}5$ litres per minute. Find the time it takes to fill the cone. Give your answer correct to the nearest second.

idea.title: Volume of a cone, and litres
idea.text: A cone holds one third of the cylinder it fits in: $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$ (tables booklet). To change cm³ to litres remember 1 litre = 1000 cm³.

steps.say: Find the volume of the cone with r = 7 and h = 12.
7² = 49, and a third of 49 × 12 is 196.
The pipe gives 0.5 litres a minute. One litre is 1000 cm³, so that is 500 cm³ every minute.
Divide the volume by 500 to get the time in minutes.
Multiply by 60 to change to seconds, then round. So it takes 74 seconds to fill the cone.

parts.tip: Get the units to match before dividing: cm³ with cm³ (1 litre = 1000 cm³).

questions.topic: Sphere in a cylinder (water level drop, curved surface); margin of error
questions.fig: (a) A sphere sitting in a cylinder full of water, then the cylinder without the sphere; a 35 cm by 20 cm metal sheet with an 18 cm-high rectangle (the cylinder's curved surface) marked out.

parts.q: A solid sphere of radius 3 cm is placed inside a cylinder and then water is poured into the cylinder until it is full, as shown in the diagram. Find the volume of the sphere, in terms of $\pi$.

idea.title: Volume of a sphere
idea.text: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ (tables booklet). 'In terms of $\pi$' means keep $\pi$ as a letter in the answer.

steps.say: Put r = 3 into the sphere formula.
3³ = 27, and four-thirds of 27 is 36. Leave π as it is. So the volume is 36π cm³.

parts.q: The sphere is now removed. The internal radius of the cylinder is 5 cm. Find the drop, in cm, in the height of the water.

idea.title: Displaced water
idea.text: When the sphere comes out, the water falls by exactly the volume of the sphere. That missing water is a thin cylinder, with the cylinder's radius and a height equal to the drop.

steps.say: The water that 'disappears' is a short cylinder of radius 5 and height h (the drop). Its volume equals the sphere's volume, 36π.
5² = 25, so 25πh = 36π. Divide both sides by 25π — the π's cancel.
So the water drops by 1.44 cm.

parts.tip: Volume removed = volume of water 'lost': set the two volumes equal.

parts.q: The cylinder has a height of 18 cm. The curved surface of the cylinder is cut from a rectangular piece of metal measuring 35 cm by 20 cm, as shown. Find how much metal will be left over when the curved surface of the cylinder is cut out. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

idea.title: Curved surface area of a cylinder
idea.text: Unroll the side of a cylinder and you get a rectangle: one side is the height $h$, the other is the circumference $2\pi r$. So its area is $2\pi r h$.

steps.say: Find the curved surface area of the cylinder: r = 5, h = 18.
Find the area of the whole metal sheet: 35 × 20.
Left over = sheet minus the part cut out. Round to 1 decimal place. So 134.5 cm² of metal is left over.

parts.q: In September 2018 a European Commission report stated that it is considering a proposal to abolish daylight saving time. This would mean that the clocks would not go forward one hour in March and then not go back one hour the following October. A Transition Year class carried out a survey to find out local people's views on the proposal. The class surveyed a random sample of 800 people in the local area. Find the margin of error of the survey. Give your answer as a percentage, correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: Margin of error
idea.text: For a random sample of $n$ people, the margin of error is about $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$.

steps.say: Use the margin of error formula with n = 800.
Multiply by 100 for a percentage and round to 2 decimal places. So the margin of error is 3.54%.

parts.q: In the survey 350 people said they supported the EU proposal to abolish daylight saving time. Use your answer to part (b)(i) above to create a 95% confidence interval for the percentage of the population who supported the EU proposal.

steps.say: Find the sample percentage: 350 out of 800.
Go 3.54% below and above it. So the 95% confidence interval is from 40.21% to 47.29%.

parts.q: A local newspaper had reported that 50% of people in the area supported the EU proposal. Use your answer to part (b)(ii) above to conduct a hypothesis test, at the 5% level of significance, to test the newspaper's claim. Clearly state your conclusion in the context of the question and give a reason for your conclusion.

options: Reject the newspaper's claim: support is not 50%
Accept the newspaper's claim: support is 50%

parts.scheme: $H_0$: the level of support is 50%; $H_1$: it is not 50%. $50\% \notin [40.21\%, 47.29\%]$, so reject $H_0$: the level of support in the area is not 50%.

idea.title: Testing a claim with a confidence interval
idea.text: If the claimed value lies inside the 95% confidence interval, it is believable; if it lies outside, reject it.

steps.say: State the null hypothesis (the newspaper's claim) and the alternative.
Is 50% inside the interval 40.21% to 47.29%? No — it is above it.
So reject the null hypothesis: the evidence says the level of support in the area is not 50%, so the newspaper's claim is rejected.

parts.tip: The reason is the key mark: '50% is not inside the confidence interval'.

questions.topic: Net of a cylindrical can; rise in water level from ice cubes
questions.stem: A rectangular sheet of aluminium is used to make a cylindrical can of radius $r$ cm and height 10 cm, as shown below. The aluminium does not overlap in the finished can.
questions.fig: A rectangle 16 cm tall and $y$ cm wide: two circles of radius $r$ side by side across the top, and a 10 cm-tall rectangle (the side of the can) along the bottom; an arrow to the finished cylinder. In (b) a cylinder of water with three spherical ice cubes added and the rise $h$ marked.

parts.q: Show that $r$, the radius of the cylinder, is 3 cm.

answer.show: Height of sheet: 10 + diameter = 16, so diameter = 6 and r = 3 cm

idea.title: Reading a net
idea.text: A net is the flat shape that folds up into the solid. Every length on the net matches a length on the solid, so you can set up equations from the sheet's measurements.

steps.say: Look up the right-hand side of the sheet: it is 16 cm. It is made of the 10 cm rectangle plus a circle standing on top of it, and the circle is one diameter tall.
So the diameter is 6 cm, and the radius is half of that: 3 cm.

parts.q: Find the distance $y$. Give your answer correct to the nearest centimetre.

idea.title: The side of a can is a rectangle
idea.text: When the side of a can is unrolled, its length is the distance around the circle — the circumference, $2\pi r$.

steps.say: The bottom rectangle wraps round the can exactly once, so its length y is the circumference of the circle.
Put in r = 3 and round. So y is 19 cm.

parts.q: Find the area, in $\text{cm}^2$, of the waste aluminium after the top, bottom and side of the cylindrical can have been removed from the rectangular sheet. Give your answer correct to the nearest $\text{cm}^2$.

steps.say: Area of the whole sheet: length y = 6π, height 16.
Area of the side (the bottom rectangle): 6π by 10.
Area of the top and bottom: two circles, each π × 3².
Waste = sheet minus the pieces used.
Work it out and round. So about 57 cm² is wasted.

parts.tip: Keep y as 6π (not the rounded 19) so your answer isn't thrown off.

parts.q: Find the volume of a spherical ice cube of radius $1{\cdot}5$ cm. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$.
parts.scheme: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi(1.5)^3 = \frac{4}{3} \times \frac{27}{8}\pi = \frac{9}{2}\pi$ cm³. (14.137 cm³, not in terms of $\pi$, gets partial credit.)

idea.title: Volume of a sphere
idea.text: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$. Keep $\pi$ as a letter when asked for the answer 'in terms of $\pi$'.

steps.say: Put r = 1.5 into the sphere formula.
1.5³ = 3.375, and four-thirds of 3.375 is 4.5. Keep the π. So the volume is 4.5π (= 9π/2) cm³.

parts.q: Three of the spherical ice cubes of radius $1{\cdot}5$ cm are added to a cylinder of internal radius $3{\cdot}5$ cm which is partially filled with water. All of the ice cubes are completely submerged in the water and the water does not overflow. Find the rise, $h$ cm, in the water level. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.scheme: Volume of risen water = volume of ice added: $\pi(3.5)^2 h = 3 \times \frac{9}{2}\pi$; $h = \frac{27}{2(3.5)^2} = 1.102 \approx 1.1$ cm.

idea.title: Water rises by the volume put in
idea.text: Anything sunk in the water pushes the level up by its own volume. The extra water forms a short cylinder with the cylinder's radius and a height equal to the rise.

steps.say: Three ice cubes go in, so the added volume is 3 × 4.5π = 13.5π.
The water rises by a cylinder of radius 3.5 and height h. Set its volume equal to 13.5π.
3.5² = 12.25. Divide both sides by 12.25π — the π's cancel.
Round to 1 decimal place. So the water rises by 1.1 cm.

parts.tip: Rise problems: (volume of cylinder with height h) = (volume dropped in).

questions.topic: Trapezoidal rule (lake); hemisphere and cone (buoy); cosine rule
questions.stem: The diagram on the right shows the plan of a lake. The line segment $[PQ]$ represents the distance from the pier, $P$, to the far side of the lake. At equal intervals of 10 m along this line, perpendicular measures are made to the sides of the lake as shown.
questions.fig: Plan of a lake with line [PQ] and offsets every 10 m. Offsets (above + below the line): at P 0 + 10, then 20 + 20, 10 + 20, 30 + 20, 30 + 10, 20 + 20, and 0 at Q. Later: a hemisphere of radius 21 cm, a buoy (cone on a hemisphere, total height $h$), and triangle PBQ with |PB| = 43 m, |BQ| = 26 m, |PQ| = 60 m.

parts.q: Use the Trapezoidal Rule to estimate the surface area of the lake.

idea.title: Trapezoidal rule with offsets on both sides
idea.text: When measurements go both above and below a line, add them to get the full width of the lake at each point. Then use the rule: Area $\approx \frac{h}{2}[\text{first} + \text{last} + 2(\text{the rest})]$.

steps.say: At each point add the measurement above the line to the one below, to get the total width of the lake there.
The gaps along [PQ] are 10 m, so h = 10. The first width is 10 and the last is 0.
The middle widths add to 200; doubled that is 400.
So the surface area of the lake is about 2050 m².

parts.tip: Write the list of heights in order before you start; it makes the formula easy to fill in.

parts.q: If the lake is on average 8 m deep, estimate the volume of water in the lake.

steps.say: Think of the lake as a slab: area of the top × depth.
So the lake holds about 16 400 m³ of water.

parts.q: Calculate the volume, in $\text{cm}^3$, of a hemisphere of radius 21 cm. Give your answer terms of $\pi$.
parts.scheme: $V = \frac{2}{3}\pi(21)^3 = 6174\pi$ cm³. (19 396 cm³, not in terms of $\pi$, loses 1 mark.)

idea.title: Volume of a hemisphere
idea.text: A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its volume is half of $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$: $V = \frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$.

steps.say: Use the hemisphere formula with r = 21.
21³ = 9261, and two-thirds of 9261 is 6174. Keep π. So the volume is 6174π cm³.

parts.q: A buoy on the lake is in the shape of a hemisphere of radius 21 cm surmounted by a cone. The volume of the cone is equal to the volume of the hemisphere. Find $h$, the total height of the buoy.

idea.title: Finding a height from a volume
idea.text: Write the cone's volume formula, set it equal to the volume you know, and solve for the height.

steps.say: The cone sits on the hemisphere, so it has the same radius, 21 cm. Its volume equals the hemisphere's, 6174π.
A third of 21² is 147. Divide both sides by 147π.
The total height is the cone's height plus the depth of the hemisphere, which is its radius 21.
So the buoy is 63 cm tall.

parts.tip: Don't forget to add the hemisphere's height (its radius) at the end — the question asks for the TOTAL height.

parts.q: The buoy is situated at $B$, 43 m from the pier $P$ and 26 m from the point $Q$, as shown in the diagram above. Find $|\angle QBP|$, the angle at the buoy shown on the diagram. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
parts.scheme: $60^2 = 26^2 + 43^2 - 2(26)(43)\cos A$; $\cos A = \frac{26^2 + 43^2 - 60^2}{2(26)(43)} = -\frac{25}{52}$; $A = 118.74^\circ$. Treating it as right-angled or using the Sine Rule gets zero.

idea.title: The cosine rule for an angle
idea.text: If you know all three sides of a triangle, the cosine rule finds any angle: $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$, where $a$ is the side opposite the angle you want.

steps.say: The angle at B is opposite the side PQ = 60. The other two sides are 26 and 43. Write the cosine rule.
Rearrange to get cos A on its own.
That gives a negative number, which means the angle is more than 90°.
Use shift-cos (cos⁻¹) with the calculator in degrees. So the angle at the buoy is 118.74°.

parts.tip: Make sure your calculator is in degrees (D), not radians.

questions.topic: Lighthouse: hemisphere and cylinder, cut-off cone, area of a circle
questions.stem: The top of a particular lighthouse is in the shape of a hemisphere on top of a cylinder. The hemisphere and the cylinder both have a radius of 3 m.
questions.fig: A hemisphere on a cylinder of height $h$, radius 3 m (and a photo). In (b) a cone of base radius 7·5 m and height 47 m with base angle $A$, then the same cone with its top cut off at a circle of radius 3 m, leaving height $k$. In (d) a ship $S$, the lighthouse top $F$ 49 m up, angle of elevation 1·2°, horizontal distance $d$.

parts.q: Find the volume of the hemisphere. Give your answer in $\text{m}^3$ in terms of $\pi$.
parts.scheme: $V = \frac{2}{3}\pi(3)^3 = 18\pi$ m³. (Answer not in terms of $\pi$ gets high partial credit.)

idea.title: Volume of a hemisphere
idea.text: A hemisphere is half a sphere, so $V = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$.

steps.say: Use the hemisphere formula with r = 3.
3³ = 27, and two-thirds of 27 is 18. Keep π. So the volume is 18π m³.

parts.tip: 'In terms of π' — leave the π in your answer.

parts.q: The volume of the cylinder is $36\pi\ \text{m}^3$. Work out $h$, the height of the cylinder.

idea.title: Missing height of a cylinder
idea.text: Volume of a cylinder is $\pi r^2 h$. If the volume is given, set $\pi r^2 h$ equal to it and solve for $h$.

steps.say: Write the cylinder's volume formula, put in r = 3, and set it equal to 36π.
3² = 9, so 9πh = 36π. Divide both sides by 9π.
So the height of the cylinder is 4 m.

parts.tip: When both sides have π, it cancels — no calculator needed.

parts.q: The diagram on the right below shows part of the base of the lighthouse (not to scale). It is in the shape of a cone of radius $7{\cdot}5$ m, from which the top part has been removed, leaving a horizontal circle of radius 3 m. The height of the cone before the top part is removed is 47 m. Work out the size of the angle at the base of the cone, marked $A$ in the diagram above. Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

idea.title: Tan in a right-angled triangle
idea.text: In a right-angled triangle, $\tan(\text{angle}) = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$. If you know both sides, shift-tan gives the angle.

steps.say: Cut the cone down the middle: the height 47, the radius 7.5 and the slope make a right-angled triangle. The side opposite A is 47; the side next to A is 7.5.
Use shift-tan (tan⁻¹) in degree mode, then round. So A is 81°.

parts.q: Find the distance marked $k$ on the diagram, the height after the top part is removed.

answer.show: 28.2 m (28.06 m using tan 81° also accepted)

idea.title: Similar triangles in a cone
idea.text: The small cone cut off the top has the same shape as the big cone, just smaller. So its height and radius are in the same ratio as the big cone's.

steps.say: Let x be the height of the small cone that was removed. Its radius is 3; the big cone's radius is 7.5 and height 47. Same shape, so the ratios match.
Multiply both sides by 47.
k is what is left of the 47 m once the top 18.8 m is removed. So k is 28.2 m.

parts.q: Assume that the Fastnet lighthouse can be seen from anywhere within a circle of radius 50 km. Work out the area of the circle within which the Fastnet lighthouse can be seen. Give your answer correct to the nearest $\text{km}^2$.

idea.title: Area of a circle
idea.text: Area of a circle $= \pi r^2$: square the radius, then multiply by $\pi$.

steps.say: Use the area formula with r = 50.
Work it out and round. So the lighthouse can be seen over about 7854 km².

parts.q: 50 km = 27 nautical miles. Use this to work out how many km are in 1 nautical mile. Give your answer correct to 4 significant figures.

steps.say: 27 nautical miles is 50 km. To find 1 nautical mile, divide by 27.
4 significant figures means keep the first four digits: 1, 8, 5, 1 — and the next digit (8) rounds it up. So 1 nautical mile is 1.852 km.

parts.tip: Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit, not from the decimal point.

parts.q: The top of the Fastnet lighthouse, $F$, is 49 m above sea level. The angle of elevation of the top of the lighthouse from a ship $S$ is $1{\cdot}2^\circ$, as shown in the diagram below (not to scale). Find the horizontal distance marked $d$ below, from the ship to the base of the lighthouse. Give your answer in kilometres, correct to 2 decimal places.

steps.say: In the right-angled triangle, 49 m is opposite the 1.2° angle and d is next to it. Use tan.
Swap d and tan 1.2° to get d on its own.
Change metres to kilometres (÷ 1000) and round. So the ship is 2.34 km away.

parts.tip: The question wants kilometres — don't stop at 2339 m.

questions.topic: Volume of a prism-shaped shed; slant length of the roof
questions.stem: Seán has built a shed. The diagrams below show the dimensions of Seán's shed. The shed is in the shape of a prism. Its front face is in the shape of a triangle on top of a rectangle. Its highest point is directly above the centre of its base.
questions.fig: Front face: a 12 m wide, 7 m high rectangle with a triangular roof; highest point 8·5 m. Whole shed: a prism 18 m long. Later: the roof's slant length $d$; a scale diagram of the front with point A; triangle ABC with |AB| = 3 m, |AC| = 7 m, angle A = 30°.

parts.q: State which of the following statements is most likely to be true, and write down a possible height of Seán that would support your answer. Tick (✓) one box only. The shed at the highest point is 3 times as high as Seán. / The shed at the highest point is 5 times as high as Seán. / The shed at the highest point is 8 times as high as Seán.

steps.say: Test each choice by dividing the shed's height, 8.5 m, by the number. That gives Seán's height.
2.83 m is far too tall for a person and 1.06 m is a small child. 1.7 m is a normal adult height. So tick '5 times', with Seán about 1.7 m tall.

parts.tip: Know rough real-life sizes: an adult is about 1.5–1.9 m tall.

parts.q: Seán says that his shed has a capacity of over one million litres, where $1\ \text{m}^3 = 1000$ litres. Work out the volume of Seán's shed, to show that he is correct.

idea.title: Volume of a prism
idea.text: A prism has the same shape all the way through, like a loaf of sliced bread. Its volume is the area of the front face × the length.

steps.say: Find the area of the front face. The rectangle is 12 by 7.
The roof triangle has base 12 and height 8.5 − 7 = 1.5. Area is half base × height.
Add them for the whole front face.
Volume of the prism = face × length, and the length is 18 m.
Change to litres: each m³ is 1000 litres. 1 674 000 is more than one million, so Seán is right.

parts.tip: The triangle's height is only the part above the rectangle: 8.5 − 7.

parts.q: Use the theorem of Pythagoras to find the length of the distance marked $d$ in the diagram below, the slant length of the roof. Give your answer in metres, correct to 1 decimal place.

idea.title: Pythagoras
idea.text: In a right-angled triangle: (longest side)² = (one short side)² + (other short side)².

steps.say: The top point is above the centre, so half the roof makes a right-angled triangle: across 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m, up 8.5 − 7 = 1.5 m, and the slope d.
Use Pythagoras.
Take the square root and round. So the slant length of the roof is 6.2 m.

parts.q: A scale diagram of the front of the shed is shown below. One point on the diagram is marked A. Construct an enlargement of the diagram below, with centre A and a scale factor of 3. Show all of your construction lines clearly.

answer.show: Draw rays from A through each corner; mark each image point 3 times as far from A; join them to get the shed shape 3 times bigger.

parts.scheme: Rays from A through each vertex with image points at 3 times the distance (e.g. |AB| ≈ 4.0 cm, |AC| ≈ 4.6 cm, |AD| ≈ 3.5 cm, |AE| ≈ 2.4 cm before enlarging); image drawn and labelled.

idea.title: Enlargement from a centre
idea.text: In an enlargement with centre A and scale factor 3, every point moves along the line from A, ending up 3 times as far from A as it was.

steps.say: From A, draw a long straight line (ray) through each corner of the shed shape.
Measure the distance from A to a corner, multiply by 3, and mark the new point on the same ray at that distance.
Do this for every corner, then join the new points in the same order. Keep all rays showing.

parts.tip: Corners that lie on A's own lines (like the bottom-right corner) still need a ray — label every image point.

parts.q: The diagram below shows part of the roof of a smaller shed (not to scale). Some measurements are marked on the diagram. Show that $|BC| = 4{\cdot}65$ m, correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.scheme: $x^2 = 3^2 + 7^2 - 2(3)(7)\cos 30^\circ = 21.6269$; $x = 4.65047 = 4.65$. Treating it as right-angled gets zero.

idea.title: The cosine rule for a side
idea.text: If you know two sides and the angle between them, the third side comes from $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$.

steps.say: BC is opposite the 30° angle, which sits between the sides 3 and 7. Use the cosine rule.
Work it out in degree mode.
Square root and round: that shows |BC| = 4.65 m.

parts.q: Find $|\angle ACB|$, the angle that the roof makes at the point $C$. Give your answer correct to the nearest degree. Remember that $|BC| = 4{\cdot}65$ m, correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: The sine rule
idea.text: In any triangle, each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same number: $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B}$.

steps.say: Angle C is opposite the 3 m side, and 30° is opposite the 4.65 m side. Use the sine rule.
Multiply both sides by 3.
Use shift-sin and round. So the roof makes an angle of 19° at C.

questions.topic: Area of a garden and pond (trapezoidal rule); cost; import duty and exchange
questions.stem: A rectangular garden (50 m by 30 m) contains an irregularly shaped pond of length 18 m, as shown in the diagram below (not to scale).
questions.fig: A 50 m by 30 m rectangle containing a pond 18 m long. Widths every 3 m from the left point: 0, 10, 14, 12, 10, 8, and 2 m at the right-hand edge.

parts.q: Find the area of the whole garden (that is, the total area of the rectangle).

idea.title: Area of a rectangle
idea.text: Area = length × width. It is measured in square units, here m².

steps.say: Multiply the length by the width.
So the garden's area is 1500 m².

parts.tip: Write the units (m²) — a mark is lost without them.

parts.q: The width of the pond is measured at intervals of 3 metres, starting at the right-hand edge of the pond. These measurements are given on the diagram, correct to the nearest metre. Use the Trapezoidal Rule (and the measurements in the diagram above) to work out an estimate for the area of the pond.

idea.title: The trapezoidal rule
idea.text: Area $\approx \frac{h}{2}[\text{first} + \text{last} + 2(\text{everything in between})]$, where $h$ is the gap between the measurements. It is in the tables booklet.

steps.say: The gap between measurements is 3 m, so h = 3. Read the widths in order: 0 at the pointed left end, then 10, 14, 12, 10, 8, and 2 at the right-hand edge.
First and last are 0 and 2; the five in between are doubled.
The middle ones add to 54, doubled is 108.
So the pond's area is about 165 m².

parts.tip: The pointed end counts as a height of 0 — don't leave it out.

parts.q: Suggest a way by which the Trapezoidal Rule could be used (with different measurements) to get a potentially more accurate estimate of the area of the pond.

answer.show: Use more strips: take the widths at smaller intervals (e.g. every 1 m), or measure the widths more accurately.

parts.scheme: Make more divisions (smaller intervals), or measure more accurately.

steps.say: The rule replaces each curved strip with a straight-sided trapezium. Thinner strips follow the curved edge more closely, so the error gets smaller.
So: measure the width at smaller intervals (more strips), or measure the widths more accurately than to the nearest metre.

parts.q: Apart from the pond, the rest of the rectangular garden is covered in grass. The actual area of the pond is $172\ \text{m}^2$. All of the grass in the garden needs to be resown. The cost is €2·55 per square metre that needs to be resown. Work out the cost of resowing the grass. Give your answer correct to the nearest ten euro.

steps.say: The grass is the garden without the pond. Use the actual pond area, 172 m².
Each square metre costs €2.55.
To the nearest ten euro, 3386.40 is closer to 3390 than 3380. So it costs about €3390.

parts.tip: 'Nearest ten euro' means the answer ends in 0.

parts.q: Some materials were imported from England by the gardener for resowing the grass. The cost of the materials was £840. This included an Import Duty of 16·9%. Work out the cost of the materials before the Import Duty was added. Give your answer correct to the nearest penny (that is, to 2 decimal places).

idea.title: Working back from a price that includes a percentage
idea.text: If 16.9% was added, the £840 is 116.9% of the original price. Find 1% (÷ 116.9), then 100% (× 100).

steps.say: The original price is 100%. Adding 16.9% makes £840 equal to 116.9%.
Divide by 116.9 to get 1%, then multiply by 100 to get the original.
Round to the nearest penny. So the materials cost £718.56 before duty.

parts.tip: Don't take 16.9% OFF £840 — that gives the wrong answer, because the 16.9% was of the smaller original price.

parts.q: The gardener paid the £840 in euro. The exchange rate was €1 = £0·8547. He also paid a fee of 2·5% of the £840 as a commission. Work out how much he paid in total, in euro, correct to the nearest cent.

steps.say: Add the 2.5% commission: he pays 102.5% of £840.
Change pounds to euro: each €1 buys £0.8547, so divide by 0.8547.
So he paid €1007.37 in total.

parts.tip: €1 = £0.8547: going from £ to € you DIVIDE by 0.8547.

questions.topic: Circles inside and outside a square: radius, area, circumference
questions.stem: The diagram below (not to scale) shows a square with sides of length 12 cm. The circle $c$ is inside the square, and touches the four sides of the square. The circle $k$ is outside the square, and goes through the four corners of the square.
questions.fig: A 12 cm square with circle $c$ touching its four sides inside, and circle $k$ passing through its four corners outside.

parts.q: Find the length of the radius of the circle $c$.

idea.title: A circle that fits inside a square
idea.text: If a circle touches all four sides of a square, it stretches right across the square. So its diameter equals the side of the square.

steps.say: Circle c touches the left and right sides, so its diameter is the side of the square, 12 cm.
The radius is half of that. So the radius of c is 6 cm.

parts.q: Work out the area of the circle $c$. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.scheme: Area $= \pi r^2 = \pi(6)^2 = 36\pi = 113.097 = 113.10$ cm². (In terms of $\pi$, wrong rounding or no units: lose 1 mark.)

idea.title: Area of a circle
idea.text: Area $= \pi r^2$: square the radius, then multiply by $\pi$.

steps.say: Use the area formula with r = 6.
Work it out and round to 2 decimal places. So the area of c is 113.10 cm².

parts.tip: 2 decimal places means 113.10, keep the 0.

parts.q: Work out the percentage of the area of the square that is taken up by the circle $c$, correct to the nearest percent.

steps.say: Find the area of the square: 12 × 12.
Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100.
Round to the nearest percent. So the circle takes up about 79% of the square.

parts.q: Show that the radius of the circle $k$ is $8{\cdot}49$ cm, correct to 2 decimal places.

answer.show: Diagonal² = 12² + 12² = 288, diagonal = 16.97; radius = 16.97 ÷ 2 = 8.49 cm (or r² = 6² + 6² = 72, r = √72 = 8.49)

idea.title: A circle through the corners of a square
idea.text: If a circle passes through all four corners, its diameter is the square's diagonal. Pythagoras finds the diagonal.

steps.say: From the centre of the square to a corner is the radius of k. It is the slope of a right-angled triangle with sides 6 and 6 (half the square each way).
Work out and take the square root.
Round to 2 decimal places: that shows the radius of k is 8.49 cm.

parts.q: Work out the circumference of the circle $k$, correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.scheme: $2\pi r = 2\pi(8.49) = 53.344 = 53.34$ cm. (53.3 without work gets zero.)

idea.title: Circumference
idea.text: The circumference is the distance around a circle: $C = 2\pi r$.

steps.say: Use C = 2πr with r = 8.49.
Work it out and round to 2 decimal places. So the circumference of k is 53.34 cm.

parts.tip: Show the formula with the numbers put in — '53.3' with no work got zero here.

questions.topic: Cylindrical paddling pool: volume, water rise; conical cover and its net
questions.stem: A family decides to buy a small paddling pool for their back garden. The pool is in the shape of a cylinder. It has an internal diameter of $2{\cdot}4$ m and an internal depth of $0{\cdot}9$ m.
questions.fig: Photo of a round paddling pool, diameter 2·4 m, depth 0·9 m. A cube-shaped seat. A wide, flat cone (radius 1·3 m, height 0·8 m, slant $l$). The cone's net: a large sector of radius $x$ with angle $A$.

parts.q: The instruction manual recommends that the pool should be filled to a maximum depth of $0{\cdot}75$ m. Work out the volume of water in the pool when it is filled to this maximum depth. Give your answer in $\text{m}^3$, correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: Volume of a cylinder
idea.text: A cylinder is a circle stretched upwards, so its volume is (area of the circle) × height: $V = \pi r^2 h$. The water only goes to the depth it is filled to.

steps.say: The diameter is 2.4 m, so the radius is 1.2 m. The water is 0.75 m deep, so use h = 0.75 (not 0.9).
Put them into the cylinder volume formula.
Work it out and round to 2 decimal places. So there is 3.39 m³ of water.

parts.tip: Use the depth of the WATER, not the depth of the pool.

parts.q: The family buys 3 pool seats. Each pool seat is a cube, with sides of length $0{\cdot}5$ m. Show that the total volume of the 3 pool seats is $0{\cdot}375\ \text{m}^3$.

idea.title: Volume of a cube
idea.text: A cube is a box with all sides equal, so its volume is side × side × side.

steps.say: Find the volume of one cube: length × width × height, all 0.5.
There are 3 seats, so multiply by 3. That gives 0.375 m³, as required.

parts.q: The pool is filled with water to a height of $0{\cdot}6$ m. The 3 pool seats are put into the pool, so that each seat is fully covered in water. Find the amount by which the water level in the pool rises. Give your answer in metres, correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: Water rises by the volume put in
idea.text: The seats push the water up by exactly their own volume. The extra water is a thin cylinder with the pool's radius and a height equal to the rise.

steps.say: The rise in water is a short cylinder of radius 1.2 and height h. Its volume equals the seats' volume, 0.375 m³.
π × 1.2² is about 4.524. Divide both sides by it.
Round to 2 decimal places. So the water rises by 0.08 m (about 8 cm).

parts.tip: The 0.6 m starting depth doesn't matter — only the volume added does.

parts.q: The family also buys a cover for the pool, to help keep the water clean. It is in the shape of a right circular cone, with a radius of $1{\cdot}3$ m and a vertical height of $0{\cdot}8$ m. Show that the slant height of the cone, marked $l$ in the diagram above, is $1{\cdot}53$ m, correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: Slant height of a cone
idea.text: The height, the radius and the slant height of a cone form a right-angled triangle, so $l^2 = h^2 + r^2$.

steps.say: Use Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle inside the cone.
Square root and round: that shows l = 1.53 m.

parts.q: Work out the curved surface area of the conical cover. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: Curved surface area of a cone
idea.text: The sloping surface of a cone has area $\pi r l$, where $l$ is the slant height.

steps.say: Use πrl with r = 1.3 and l = 1.53.
Work it out and round. So the cover's curved area is 6.25 m².

parts.q: The diagram below shows the net of the conical cover (not to scale). It is a sector of a circle of radius $x$. Write down the value of $x$ and work out the size of the angle $A$, correct to the nearest degree.
parts.scheme: $x = 1.53$ m. Area of sector = CSA: $\frac{A}{360} \times \pi(1.53)^2 = 6.25$, $A = 305.9 \approx 306^\circ$. Or arc = base circumference: $\frac{A}{360} \times 2\pi(1.53) = 2\pi(1.3)$, $A = \frac{1.3 \times 360}{1.53} = 306^\circ$.

idea.title: The net of a cone is a sector
idea.text: Unroll a cone's side and you get a sector. Its radius is the slant height. Its curved edge wraps around the base, so arc length = $2\pi r$ of the base.

steps.say: The sector's radius is the slant height of the cone, so x = 1.53 m.
The arc of the sector wraps round the base circle of radius 1.3. The arc is the fraction A/360 of the full circle of radius 1.53.
The 2π cancels on both sides, leaving a simple fraction.
Work it out and round. So x = 1.53 m and A = 306°.

parts.tip: A big flat cone gives a net that is nearly a full circle — 306° makes sense.

questions.topic: Tennis balls: speed conversion, sphere surface area and volume, cylinder and box
questions.fig: A tennis ball (sphere); a cross-section showing an outer radius $r_1$ and inner radius $r_2$ (the rubber layer); three balls stacked in a closed cylinder of height $h$; the same three balls in a closed rectangular box.

parts.q: In Wimbledon Tennis Tournament 2023, the fastest women's serve was by Aryna Sabalenka at 121 miles per hour. (Source www.wimbledon.org) Use the conversion rate of 1 mile = $1{\cdot}61$ km to convert 121 miles to km.

steps.say: Each mile is 1.61 km, so 121 miles is 121 lots of 1.61 km: multiply.
So 121 miles is 194.81 km.

parts.q: Convert one hour to seconds.

steps.say: An hour has 60 minutes, and each minute has 60 seconds.
So one hour is 3600 seconds.

parts.q: Use your answers to parts (a)(i) and (a)(ii) to convert 121 miles per hour to metres per second. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: Changing units of speed
idea.text: Speed is distance ÷ time. Change the distance to metres and the time to seconds, then divide.

steps.say: In one hour the ball would go 194.81 km. Change that to metres: × 1000.
One hour is 3600 seconds, so divide the metres by 3600.
Round to 2 decimal places. So the serve was 54.11 m/s.

parts.q: Tennis balls are in the shape of a sphere. For professional tennis matches, tennis balls can be of slightly different sizes. The smallest size allowed has a radius of $3{\cdot}27$ cm. Find the surface area of this tennis ball. Give your answer in $\text{cm}^2$, correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: Surface area of a sphere
idea.text: The surface of a sphere has area $4\pi r^2$ (tables booklet).

steps.say: Use the sphere surface area formula with r = 3.27.
Work it out and round to 2 decimal places. So the surface area is 134.37 cm².

parts.q: The cross-section of a tennis ball is shown in the diagram on the right. The ball is made up of an air-filled centre and a rubber layer of uniform thickness. The external radius ($r_1$) of the tennis ball is $3{\cdot}4$ cm. The internal radius ($r_2$) of the rubber layer is $3{\cdot}1$ cm. Find the volume of the rubber layer. Give your answer in $\text{cm}^3$, correct to 2 decimal places.

idea.title: Volume of a hollow ball
idea.text: The rubber is the whole ball with the air in the middle taken out. So its volume = (big sphere) − (small sphere).

steps.say: Find the volume of the whole ball, radius 3.4.
Find the volume of the air in the middle, radius 3.1.
Subtract to get the rubber, and round. So the rubber layer is 39.85 cm³.

parts.tip: Don't subtract the radii first (3.4 − 3.1) and cube that — that is a different, wrong volume.

parts.q: The diagram on the right shows the smallest closed cylindrical container that contains three identical tennis balls, arranged one directly on top of the other. The radius of each tennis ball is $3{\cdot}4$ cm. The height of the cylinder is $h$. Show that $h = 20{\cdot}4$ cm.

answer.show: Each ball is 2 × 3.4 = 6.8 cm tall; 3 balls: 3 × 6.8 = 20.4 cm (that is 6 radii: 3.4 × 6 = 20.4)

steps.say: Each ball is one diameter tall: 2 × 3.4 = 6.8 cm.
The three balls are stacked with no gaps, touching the top and bottom, so the height is three diameters. That shows h = 20.4 cm.

parts.q: Hence, calculate the volume of the cylinder. Give your answer correct to nearest whole number.

idea.title: Volume of a cylinder
idea.text: $V = \pi r^2 h$: the area of the circular end × the height.

steps.say: The cylinder fits the balls exactly, so its radius is 3.4 and its height is 20.4.
Work it out and round to the nearest whole number. So the cylinder holds 741 cm³.

parts.q: The three tennis balls could also be arranged, one directly on top of the other, inside a closed rectangular box, as shown below. Find the surface area of the smallest such rectangular box, in $\text{cm}^2$.

idea.title: Surface area of a box
idea.text: A closed box has 6 rectangular faces in 3 matching pairs. Find the area of each different face and add them all up.

steps.say: The smallest box just fits one ball across, so its base is a square 6.8 by 6.8 (one diameter). Its height is 20.4, like the cylinder.
Top and bottom: two squares, each 6.8 × 6.8.
The four sides: each a rectangle 6.8 × 20.4.
Add them. So the box has a surface area of 647.36 cm².

parts.tip: Count the faces: a closed box has 6. Draw the net if you're unsure.
